title: How I make films in New York on an indie budget.
dek: Jugaad, a phone full of friends, and a city that works as a free set.
short: Films in New York on an indie budget

cover.alt: Still from The Last Pizza, a survival thriller written, directed and edited by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, with Nathan Flores, Chris and Yi Chan: the delivery guy alone on a New York rooftop at dusk
cover.cap: [The Last Pizza](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3YfriOGVA4w): a thriller shot on New York rooftops for $50.

body: p

I did the one-year filmmaking conservatory at the [New York Film Academy](https://www.nyfa.edu/), focused on directing. We did everything: directing, cinematography, writing, acting. Classes ran five or six days a week, and weekends were for shooting.
p

I figured out fast that I couldn't spend on my films what a lot of my classmates spent on theirs. I come from a middle-class family in India. So I did what we do back home: jugaad. Find the smart, cheap way to get it done.
h2
My budget is people
p

I made friends everywhere. Actors, musical theatre students, cinematographers, anyone in the building. I went to events and filmmaking meetups and talked about my stories with whoever would listen. So when I had a film to make, I already knew who was right for it. I called them, and because they were friends who trusted the project, they came on as collaborators.
p

Call your friends and family first. You don't have to hire every role off [Backstage](https://www.backstage.com/) or pay for an AD and a DP on day one. Your friends might be better, and every shoot turns them into a team that's there for the next one.
p

You can see it in my credits. Nathan Flores is in [The Last Pizza](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3YfriOGVA4w), [Agent X](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIja5IH9eo) and [Before We Leave](https://youtu.be/vTM1-v4kuSQ). Yi Chan (Ethan) acted in The Last Pizza, shot Before We Leave and was my AD on Agent X. Cito shot The Last Pizza and ran sound on Agent X. Same family, different films.

Today, if you asked me for a crew, I could put one together in seconds: DP, AD, actors, sound, a colorist, an editor. That's the whole trick. It's harder if you're shy, I get it. Do it anyway.
h2
Micro dramas: the same family, a bigger slate
p

The same approach carried into the micro dramas I direct for [Canvas](https://creatorsarethenewstudios.com): 12+ series so far, including [Face Value](/series/face-value/), [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/), [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/), [Taser Fight Championship](/series/taser-fight-championship/) and [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/). Each runs four to ten episodes, every episode under two minutes. The constant on every one: me directing and Abhinav Singla on production.
p

Around us, the same people keep coming back. Nishita was my AD on Dear NYC. Navya did art on Dear NYC and Red Flags. Karun shot Dear NYC, and Kais Vasaya shot most of the others, including Face Value and Demo Day. Onil Shah colored most of them and shot some too.

body: p

Actors I met making short films, like Dillon Cain from Agent X and Cassidy, came back for the micro dramas. Post is friends too. Asla, who edits for my marketing studio, has cut micro drama promos, trailers, teasers and some full episodes. Adarsh has edited with me and Advait has helped. Some of the non-fiction series were edited by friends from my [WLDD](/work/fifteen-people-on-one-floor/) days: Madhur, Karthik and Tushar. And Akhand, my graphic designer from my marketing work, made most of the series posters.
p
They came from earlier sets, film school, my old office and cold DMs, not from a budget line.
h2
Cold DMs work
p

Join every community you can. I'm in New York filmmaker groups on WhatsApp and Facebook, and I meet people on Instagram all the time. When someone's work catches your eye, message them. Don't overthink what they'll think of you. A lot of my DOPs, colorists and editors started as a cold DM on Instagram, and those friends introduced me to more.
h2
New York is the set
p

My films have cost under $700, and some cost nothing. Locations come from friends too: their apartments become your sets. Outside, New York does a lot of the work. It's backlit almost everywhere you point a camera, and backlight is free production value.
p

Manhattan streets, the Brooklyn Bridge, Bryant Park, Times Square, Central Park: take a camera and go. I rewrite scenes to fit the places I can get. Subways are easy to shoot, so sometimes the scene just moves to the subway.
p

On permits: the city's film office says you generally don't need one if you're shooting with a handheld camera or a camera on a tripod, with hand-held gear, and you aren't taking over city property or using vehicles, prop weapons, stunts or actors in police uniforms. [Check the rules](https://www.nyc.gov/site/mome/permits/when-permit-required.page) before you shoot. The subway belongs to the MTA, which has [its own filming rules](https://www.mta.info/doing-business-with-us/filming).
p

If you do need one, the permit itself is free. The [Film Office](https://www.nyc.gov/site/mome/permits/when-permit-required.page) says its permits come with free police assistance, free parking privileges and access to most exterior locations at no charge. You'll need a [certificate of insurance](https://www.nyc.gov/site/mome/permits/permit-step1.page) before you apply, so plan for that cost.
h2
Pick stories your budget can carry
p

Sci-fi and action eat money. I make realistic films: people talking, drama, comedy, romance, emotions, sometimes close to non-fiction. It's the work I love, and it happens to be the work an indie budget can carry. That's why making indie films came easy to me. It's just who I am as a filmmaker.
h2
You're in good company
p
None of this is new. Spike Lee shot [She's Gotta Have It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She%27s_Gotta_Have_It) in Brooklyn in twelve days in the summer of 1985, for $175,000, with a non-union crew.
p

Over in New Jersey, Kevin Smith made [Clerks](https://www.mentalfloss.com/article/70020/18-black-and-white-facts-about-clerks) for $27,575 in the convenience store where he worked, mostly on maxed-out credit cards. His longtime friend Walt Flanagan played four different customers.
p

And the micro drama business runs on the same math. A 100-page micro drama script can be shot in about a week, against a month for a feature ([Los Angeles Times](https://www.aol.com/news/hollywoods-romance-micro-dramas-heating-100000961.html)), and whole seasons have been made for $50,000 to $250,000 with affordable, often non-union casts ([Final Draft](https://www.finaldraft.com/blog/what-are-verticals-and-micro-dramas)). Ours are shorter, and we lean even harder on the family.
p

If your actors are in the union, that doesn't have to end the conversation. SAG-AFTRA's [Micro-Budget Project Agreement](https://sagaftra.org/how-can-i-work-indie-films) covers live-action projects budgeted at $20,000 or less per picture, or per episode for a series, from shorts and features to web series. The union says the sign-up is quick enough to do [right before you start shooting](https://sagaftra.org/micro-brings-big-changes-indie-filmmaking-and-content-creation). Read the terms first: the project has to be shot in the US, and it limits where the film can be shown, to festivals, classrooms and free ad-supported platforms.
h2
Feed your crew
p
Be kind to everyone on set, and feed them. Real food, not only pizza. People remember how you treated them, and they'll come back any day you call.
h2
A checklist for your first no-budget shoot
ul
Write for what you can get. List the free places you have, a friend's apartment, a street, a park, and write the scenes into them.
Fill the crew sheet with names before you post a casting call: DP, AD, sound, actors, editor, colorist. Friends first, then their friends.
Check the [city's permit rules](https://www.nyc.gov/site/mome/permits/when-permit-required.page), and [the MTA's](https://www.mta.info/doing-business-with-us/filming) if the scene goes underground.
If an actor is in SAG-AFTRA, read the [Micro-Budget agreement](https://sagaftra.org/how-can-i-work-indie-films) before you cast.
Put someone on sound, even a friend with a recorder.
Get a signed release from everyone on camera and from every location you use.
Budget the food before anything else.
Line up the edit before the shoot, so the footage doesn't sit on a drive.
h2
Mistakes to avoid
ul
Writing the expensive version first and hoping the money shows up. Write the version you can shoot this month.
Treating friends as free labor. They're collaborators: credit them properly, feed them, and show them the cut first.
Waiting until you feel ready to message people. The cold DM you don't send is the crew you don't have.
Shooting somewhere you're not allowed. Ten minutes with the rules can save a shoot day.
Only meeting people when you need something. Go to the meetups when you have nothing to shoot.
quote
My budget was never money. It was people.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**How much does a short film cost to make in New York?** Less than you think if your budget is people. [The Last Pizza](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3YfriOGVA4w) was shot on New York rooftops for $50, and [Frames of Silence](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4IGrik_Qho) cost $696.

**Do you need a permit to film in New York City?** It depends on the shoot. Check the city's [rules on when a permit is required](https://www.nyc.gov/site/mome/permits/when-permit-required.page) before you roll.

**Can you cast SAG-AFTRA actors on a tiny budget?** Often, yes. SAG-AFTRA's [Micro-Budget Project Agreement](https://sagaftra.org/how-can-i-work-indie-films) covers live-action projects budgeted at $20,000 or less.
**How do you find a crew with no budget?** Start with friends and classmates, send the cold DMs, go to meetups when you have nothing to shoot, and feed everyone.
p

That's the short version. I'll tell the stories behind each shoot in the next few pieces. All my short films are [on the home page](/#films). If you're making something in New York and need a crew, [say hi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nivedkrishna).

title: What happened when we took Canvas to SF and LA Tech Week.
dek: Two events in three days, an Oscar-winning editor on the bill, 371 names on one guest list, and the trailers for my series in front of both rooms.
short: Canvas at SF and LA Tech Week

cover.alt: House of 434 founder Shilpi Nayak speaking to guests under string lights at The Hybrid Studio, the Canvas and House of 434 event at LA Tech Week 2026, from the after-movie of the trip by Canvas creative director Nivedkrishna Thavarayil
cover.cap: House of 434 founder Shilpi Nayak at The Hybrid Studio, LA Tech Week, October 12, 2026.

body: p

In October, Canvas went west. [Abhinav Singla](https://www.instagram.com/abhinav_singla/), our CEO, and I spent four or five days between San Francisco and Los Angeles for [SF Tech Week](https://www.tech-week.com/calendar) (October 5 to 11) and LA Tech Week (October 12 to 18), the decentralized tech conference [presented by a16z](https://www.tech-week.com/deep-tech). We hosted two events, went to plenty more, pitched Canvas every single day and still shot about four series in between.
p

I went as Canvas's creative director, with the trailers for the series I directed. This is what the week looked like from my side of the camera, who was in each room, what they said, and what it taught me about pitching stories to a room full of tech people.
h2
The short version
ul
**San Francisco:** Saturday, October 10, 1 to 4pm, at 555 Grant Ave, hosted by [Anwar Events](https://luma.com/anwar-8t0d). 371 people on the guest list.
**Los Angeles:** Monday, October 12, 5 to 8pm, at 11520 W Pico Blvd, hosted by [House of 434](https://houseof434.com/) and listed as an a16z event. About 300 people came.
**On stage:** Ilias Anwar, Abhinav Singla, Ben Woollams and Xavier Santos in SF. Shilpi Nayak, Oscar-winning editor Hemal Trivedi and Abhinav in LA.
**On screen:** the trailers for our slate, including [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/), which premiered to both rooms.

**In the can:** two after-movies and about four series, including [Young Founders](/series/young-founders/) and [Hacker Room](/series/hacker-room/) in San Francisco and [LA Artists](/series/la-artists/) in Los Angeles.

San Francisco: investing in media IP, with Anwar Events
p

"Time to show San Francisco what we've been building," Abhinav says to camera in the first second of our after-movie. On Saturday, October 10, [Ilias Anwar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/iliasanwar) and [Anwar Events](https://luma.com/anwarevents), his community of 70,000 founders, investors and creators, hosted our launch party at 555 Grant Ave. On Luma it was billed as [Canvas: Investing in content, IP, and storytelling](https://luma.com/anwar-8t0d), and 371 people were on the guest list.
p

Ilias is the CEO of [Anwar Media](https://www.anwarmedia.com/), which produces events and brand partnerships for tech companies including SpaceX and RedNote, and he moderated the panel. Next to him: Abhinav; [Ben Woollams](https://advertisingweek.com/ben-woollams-ceo-and-founder-truerights/), founder and CEO of TrueRights, a platform that helps talent license their content and likeness; and Xavier Santos, CTO of [Pinto Labs](https://pintolabs.ai/), a San Francisco team building AI-native consumer apps, backed by Caffeinated Capital and Electric Capital. The host list also included Charles Legard, Lane Spurlock, Saketh Gunda and [Shilpi Nayak](https://x.com/shilpinayak), who would host us again in Los Angeles two days later.
p

On stage, Abhinav walked the room through the slate in four lanes: fashion, travel, fiction and non-fiction. His words in the after-movie: "so many different possibilities of short-form shows across genres." Then the trailers did the talking. [The Red Carpet Show](/series/the-red-carpet-show/), the 90-second red carpet interview series I direct with Ilias as host, was filming interviews with guests.

Los Angeles: The Hybrid Studio, an a16z night with House of 434
p

"Presenting Canvas in Los Angeles" is the first line of the second after-movie. Two days later, on Monday, October 12, House of 434 hosted [The Hybrid Studio: From Oscar-Winning Films to AI-Native Studios](https://luma.com/houseof-nelv) at 11520 W Pico Blvd, with Canvas, Anwar Media, Ugly Talk and Jetzy as partners. It was an a16z event on the [LA Tech Week calendar](https://www.tech-week.com/calendar/la/events/the-hybrid-studio-from-oscar-winning-films-to-ai-native-studios-ff5fa56b-f457-4580-81fd-c353cbbdaf1a), and [dot.LA put it in its guide](https://dot.la/la-tech-week-monday-2026-2678063292.html) to Monday at LA Tech Week.
p

Shilpi Nayak opened the night. She founded [House of 434](https://houseof434.com/) and 434 VC, an early-stage fund for frontier technology, after leading engineering teams at Google and building a YC-backed startup. Then came two talks. [Hemal Trivedi](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm2578458/) presented From Oscar-Winning Filmmaking to ZeroInfinity, the company she co-founded. She edited [Saving Face](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saving_Face_%282012_film%29), which won the Oscar for Best Documentary Short, won an Emmy for that edit, and the night billed her as an AMPAS voting member and a Columbia Journalism professor. Abhinav presented Creators Are the New Studios.
p

Then the two sat down for a fireside on where craft meets AI, joined on stage by an investor in the AI video company [Higgsfield](https://higgsfield.ai/). The questions on the program are the ones every filmmaker I know is asking: where AI genuinely improves the creative process and where it falls short, whether small teams can now make what used to take a studio, and how short-form IP, distribution and ownership will change. The night closed with questions from the room.

body: h2
Two rooms, two doors
p
The slate was the same in both cities. The way in wasn't, and seeing the two side by side is the most useful thing I brought home.
ul
**The billing.** San Francisco: investing in content, IP and storytelling. Los Angeles: Oscar-winning films meet AI-native studios.
**The host.** San Francisco: a founder and investor community of 70,000. Los Angeles: a curated house for AI builders and investors, on a16z's calendar.
**The room.** San Francisco leaned investors, founders and creators. Los Angeles leaned filmmakers, AI founders and the investors who back them.
**Our angle.** San Francisco heard Canvas as infrastructure for media IP. Los Angeles heard it as proof that a small team can make studio-grade work.
**What landed.** In both rooms, the trailer did more than any slide. People asked about the shows first and the business second.
h2
Why micro dramas belong at a tech week
p

Micro dramas are a phone business before they're a film business. Sensor Tower counted [$2.98 billion in in-app revenue](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/microdrama-apps-stand-out-on-mobile-heres-what-the-numbers-say/812610/) for micro and short drama apps in 2025, up 115% on the year before, and time spent in those apps grew by 5.78 billion hours. In the first quarter of 2025, [the US alone brought in 49%](https://sensortower.com/blog/state-of-short-drama-apps-2025) of global revenue. And those apps sent [68% of their US ad spending to social networks](https://www.emarketer.com/content/microdramas-bank-on-social-ads-drive-growth) from January to September 2025, which tells you where audiences get found.
p

The creator side is just as big. Goldman Sachs Research estimated the creator economy at $250 billion in 2023 and projected [$480 billion by 2027](https://goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/the-creator-economy-could-approach-half-a-trillion-dollars-by-2027). [Tech Week's own site](https://www.tech-week.com/deep-tech) puts its attendance at more than 100,000 people across its cities. Canvas sits where the two meet: series built around creators who already have an audience, made for the phone. That's a tech story as much as a film story, so we took it to the rooms where the tech money and the AI tools are.
h2
What two rooms taught me about pitching stories to tech
ul

**Lead with the trailer, not the deck.** A deck tells a room what a show could be. A trailer shows it before anyone has time to check their phone. I'd take one good trailer over nine slides about the market, every time.

**Your positioning should fit on a hoodie.** Ours is [creators are the new studios](https://creatorsarethenewstudios.com). It's on the hoodie, on the posters and in the title of Abhinav's talk. If a line can't survive being printed on merch, it's too long.

**Same slate, different room.** San Francisco's program was about investing in media and IP. Los Angeles was about where AI meets craft. It's the same muscle I use on brand work: one product, many audiences, and each one needs its own door.
**Shoot while you pitch.** Between events we shot about four series across both cities. One trip gave us the after-movies, every photo on this page and new episodes for the slate.
**Host, don't just attend.** We partnered with hosts who already had the room: Anwar Events in San Francisco and House of 434 in Los Angeles. Their lists brought the people; we brought the work.
**Pitch every day.** Hosting took two nights. Every other day was pitching at whatever event we were at.
h2
Cutting for a loud room
p

Every Canvas episode is under two minutes and built on hooks and cliffhangers, and a trailer for a loud room needs the same build. Open on the hook, so the first seconds earn the next ones. Put the creator on screen early, because their face is the reason a stranger already cares. Close on a question, not a logo. In a room full of conversations, nobody waits for a slow build.
p

The after-movies work on the same clock. Each one runs about 40 seconds and opens on one spoken line from Abhinav before the music takes over: a promise in San Francisco, a presentation in Los Angeles. They do the job the event can't do on its own: keep working after everyone goes home.
h2
A checklist for a small team at a big tech week
ul
Pick two or three events your audience already goes to, and find a host who already has the room.
Cut trailers that still work with the sound off. Event rooms are loud.
Write one line that fits on a hoodie. Ours: creators are the new studios.
Make a one-page slate: every title, its creator and its lane.
Bring a camera, even a small crew. The after-movie keeps working long after the week ends.
Book meetings before you land. Calendars fill up fast during the week.
Follow up within two days, with the trailer link in the first line.
h2
Mistakes to avoid
ul
Bringing a deck and no footage.
Giving every room the same pitch. Keep the slate, change the way in.
Spending the whole week at panels and none of it shooting.
Treating the event as the finish line. The follow-up is the work.
Forgetting to photograph your own team. The pictures of you in the room are the ones you'll use for months.
h2
The people we met
p

We pitched to investors, filmmakers and AI filmmakers every day, and met investors including Taylor Rothchild and Ankur from [OnlyExit](https://onlyexit.pages.dev/), the Seattle hacker house and founder community. We also spent a couple of hours at director [Jeremiah S. Chechik](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0154819/)'s home in Venice, talking film. Two or three hours with the director of [National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Lampoon%27s_Christmas_Vacation) and [Benny & Joon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_%26_Joon) is not a bad way to spend part of Tech Week.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**What is Tech Week?** A decentralized tech conference presented by a16z: thousands of separate events hosted by startups, companies and VCs across a city in one week. In 2026 it ran in [Boston, New York, San Francisco and Los Angeles](https://intercom.help/tech-week-by-a16z/en/articles/14171298-what-are-the-dates-for-tech-week-2026).
**What is Canvas?** A streaming app for short series and, in its own words, infrastructure for building media IP, founded by Abhinav Singla. Its line: creators are the new studios.
**What is a micro drama?** A scripted series made for the phone, with episodes of a minute or two, each ending on a hook. Every Canvas episode I've directed runs under two minutes.

**What did Canvas show?** Trailers for the slate, sorted into fashion, travel, fiction and non-fiction, including [Face Value](/series/face-value/), [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/), [Taser Fight Championship](/series/taser-fight-championship/), [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/) and [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/).
quote
Creators are the new studios.
p

[Face Value](/series/face-value/) is already streaming on the Canvas app, and the rest of the slate is on the way. See [all 12+ series I've directed for Canvas](/#series), my [case studies and takes](/work/), or how to [work with me](/work-with-me/). If you were in either room, [say hi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/nivedkrishna).

dek: From a top floor in Bangalore to owning ScoopWhoop: what a meme agency's early team taught me.

cover.cap: About 15 people when I joined, and [about 300 by July 2026](https://manifest-media.in/special-feature/170726/spotlighting-indias-independent-companies-wldd.html).

body: p

I joined WLDD in Bangalore in January 2023, when the whole company fit on the top floor of one building. There were about fifteen of us, and I was one of the first people in that office. I started as a junior brand strategist. Two months later I was a creative strategist, working on campaigns for brands I had grown up with.
h2
Memes were the product
p

WLDD's edge was meme marketing: funny, quirky, shareable copy that people passed on because it was good, not because it was an ad. We did it for Zomato, Swiggy One, Zepto and Bingo! Mad Angles. For films, an organic meme push could put people in seats, and the audience never knew the joke they were sharing had been planned.
p

The engine was distribution. WLDD worked with hundreds of India's biggest meme pages, so one idea could land everywhere on the same day. Releases for Prime Video, Netflix India, ZEE5, Sony Pictures, Sony Music and South Indian cinema all ran through that network. By [afaqs' count](https://www.afaqs.com/news/mktg/meme-experts-the-new-specialist-agencies-on-the-block), the agency has worked with more than 120 brands on over 1,050 campaigns, with a community of more than 10,000 creators.
h2
What I made there
ul

I pitched and closed Sony Pictures as WLDD's first international client. [Our Pope's Exorcist cinema stunt](/work/the-popes-exorcist/) was covered by Hindustan Times, India Today and The Indian Express.
I worked on [Thank You Durex](/work/thank-you-durex/), a fan page we built for Durex India. One reel passed 20.9 million views, and I'm the last person in it.
I ran [WLDD's own Instagram](/work/wldd-instagram/). A typical reel went from about 4,000 views to about 19,000.
I worked on ZEE5's Taj: Divided by Blood, Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar and Kannada cinema, including PR and marketing around Yash and KGF: Chapter 2.

body: h2
Then the building filled up
p
Every few months we needed more room. We took the second floor, then the first, then the whole building. Then came a second building, for LIT School.
p

I left in 2024, at the peak of my time there, to study filmmaking in New York. WLDD kept growing. In February 2025 it [bought ScoopWhoop from The Good Glamm Group](https://www.exchange4media.com/marketing-news/the-good-glamm-group-sells-scoopwhoop-to-wldd-in-rs-20-cr-deal-141145.html) in a deal reported at Rs 20 crore. A month later it [took a majority stake in the sneaker brand 7-10](https://inc42.com/?p=505650), and in June 2025 it [acquired the creative studio Imagined](https://inc42.com/buzz/wldd-acquires-creative-studio-imagined).
p

By July 2026 it had [about 300 people across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi](https://manifest-media.in/special-feature/170726/spotlighting-indias-independent-companies-wldd.html). In September 2026, [Adfactors PR and Vikas Khemani bought a stake](https://www.exchange4media.com/pr-and-corporate-communication-news/wldd-secures-strategic-investment-from-adfactors-pr-vikas-khemani-157867.html), and Adfactors PR's CEO joined the board.
h2
What I took with me
p

That floor taught me three things I still use at [Thava Studio](https://www.instagram.com/thava.studio) in New York. Write it so people want to send it to a friend. Put it where the audience already is, not where you wish they were. And ship it while people are still talking about the thing it's about.
h2
Rule one: write it so people want to send it
p
The test I use: before anything goes out, name the friend you'd send it to. If you can't, it isn't ready.
p

Most sends come with a short message attached: this is so you, this is us, remember this? Write for that message. In my experience, a post that gives someone a reason to send it to one specific friend travels further than one that's merely good.
p

The platforms now measure exactly this. Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri, has said the [three signals that matter most in ranking](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/instagram-shares-algorithm-2025/738034/) are watch time, likes and sends, and that sends matter a little more for reaching people who don't follow you yet. The research on why people share goes back further. Jonah Berger and Katherine Milkman studied three months of New York Times articles and found that [positive content was shared more than negative](https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2011/11/Virality.pdf), and that content stirring high-arousal feelings like awe, anger or anxiety spread further, while content that made people sad spread less.
h2
Rule two: put it where the audience already is
p

WLDD didn't wait for people to find a brand's page. It worked with hundreds of meme pages, so one idea could land everywhere on the same day. Sometimes that meant building a new home for the content altogether, as you'll see below.
p
For a brand today, that means asking where your people already spend their evenings: a creator's page, a meme page, a group chat, a community. Go there with something worth sending.
h2
Rule three: ship it while people are still talking
p
A joke about last week's news is a joke nobody sends. A small team has the edge here, because fewer people need to say yes. On that top floor, the distance between an idea and a post was a few desks.
p

Speed only works with taste, though. The 2025 [Sprout Social Index](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/press/the-days-of-trend-chasing-are-over-new-research-from-sprout-social-reveals-a-third-of-consumers-think-jumping-on-viral-trends-is-embarrassing-for-brands/), a survey of 4,044 consumers in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, found that a third of them think it's embarrassing when brands jump on viral trends. Fast and off-brand is worse than late.
h2
What the rules looked like in practice
ul

Write it to be sent: for [The Pope's Exorcist](/work/the-popes-exorcist/), we put a possessed woman in a movie theater as the trailer played. It was built to be filmed and passed on, and it reached millions of people across India.

Go where the audience already is: [Thank You Durex](/work/thank-you-durex/) was a fan page we built so the memes had a home of their own, instead of running on Durex India's premium page. One reel passed 20.9 million views.

Ship it while it's live: on [WLDD's own Instagram](/work/wldd-instagram/) we turned agency news, festivals and events into reels, about one every five days, and wrote every caption to be sent to a friend. In 2022, 8 of 82 reels passed 10,000 views. In my sixteen months, 56 of 100 did.
h2
A checklist before you post
ul
Can you name the friend you'd send it to?
Does it land in the first second, without the caption?
Does the brand belong in the joke, or was it stuck on at the end?
Is the moment still alive? If people have stopped talking about it, skip it.
Is it going where the audience already is, not only on your own page?
h2
Mistakes to avoid
ul
Making an ad and calling it a meme. People can tell, and they don't send ads.
Chasing every trend. Take only the ones you can move into your brand's world.
Counting likes and ignoring sends. Likes say people enjoyed it; sends say it will travel.
Letting approvals kill the timing. Agree on taste up front, so the decision on the day is quick.
Posting only on your own page and calling it distribution.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**What is WLDD?** Wubba Lubba Dub Dub, a Bengaluru meme marketing agency founded in 2018 by Arihant Jain, Jaidev Kesti and Vivekanand Kilari. It has since bought ScoopWhoop, a majority stake in the sneaker brand 7-10 and the creative studio Imagined.
**What is meme marketing?** Brand communication written in the internet's own formats and humour, spread through meme pages and creators so it travels like content rather than an ad.

**What did I do at WLDD?** I joined in January 2023 as a junior brand strategist, became a creative strategist two months later, closed Sony Pictures as the agency's first international client and ran the agency's own Instagram until I left in 2024.
p
Fifteen desks on a top floor became a company of about 300 people that owns ScoopWhoop. I'm glad I was there when it was small enough that every idea I pitched might get made.
quote
When a team is small enough that every idea can ship, speed and taste beat budget.

title: What the Pope's Exorcist taught me about virality.
dek: And why most brands get it wrong.
body: p

In early 2023, I was a Creative Strategist at WLDD, a scrappy startup of fifteen people sharing one office in Bangalore, India. We had big clients, bigger ambitions, and the kind of energy that only exists when a company is small enough that every idea you pitch might actually get made.
p

Sony Pictures India came to us with a brief for [The Pope's Exorcist](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt13375076/), Julius Avery's horror film with Russell Crowe as Father Gabriele Amorth, the Vatican's chief exorcist. It opened in Indian cinemas on April 7, 2023, a week before the US, [in English, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu](https://www.outlookindia.com/art-entertainment/-the-pope-s-exorcist-trailer-unravels-vatical-conspiracy-through-a-young-boy-s-possession-news-264794). The ask was straightforward: generate buzz, drive awareness, get people talking.
p

What happened next was covered by [News18](https://www.news18.com/buzz/the-popes-exorcist-trailer-brings-horror-to-life-as-possessed-woman-jumps-out-in-theatre-7496905.html), [India Today](https://www.indiatoday.in/trending-news/story/woman-acts-possessed-while-trailer-of-the-popes-exorcist-plays-in-movie-theatre-video-is-viral-2357066-2023-04-07), [Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustantimes.com/trending/woman-scares-people-in-theatre-as-the-pope-s-exorcist-trailer-plays-on-screen-101680956103411.html), [The Indian Express](https://indianexpress.com/article/trending/trending-in-india/possessed-woman-growls-at-moviegoers-as-the-popes-exorcist-trailer-plays-in-theatre-8545834/) and [SheThePeople](https://www.shethepeople.tv/viral-video/woman-acts-possessed-the-popes-exorcist), reached millions of people across India, and earned WLDD its first international Hollywood client. WLDD has since grown from fifteen people to [about 300](https://manifest-media.in/special-feature/170726/spotlighting-indias-independent-companies-wldd.html), [bought ScoopWhoop](https://www.storyboard18.com/brand-makers/meme-marketing-agency-wldd-buys-scoopwhoop-from-the-good-glamm-group-in-all-cash-deal-57487.htm), and become one of India's best-known meme marketing agencies. I wrote about those early days in [I joined WLDD when it was fifteen people on one floor](/work/fifteen-people-on-one-floor/).
p

I'm not telling you this to brag. I'm telling you this because everything I learned about virality, real virality and not the manufactured kind, I learned from that campaign. And most of it runs counter to what brands are told to do.
h2
The short version
ul
**Lead with the moment, not the brand.** People share what happened to someone, not your trailer.
**Cultural fluency beats production value.** Know exactly how your audience watches, laughs and shares.
**Make someone a little nervous.** Safe ideas get approved and forgotten.
**Treat memes as a language,** not a tactic you try once.
**Move while the moment is alive.** The shorter the approval path, the better the odds.
h2
1. Virality is not about the brand. It's about the moment.
p

The biggest mistake I see brands make is putting themselves at the centre of everything they create. Their logo, their tagline, their product shot, front and centre, every single time. The audience doesn't care. The audience cares about themselves, their culture, their emotions, and what's happening in their world right now.
p

The Pope's Exorcist campaign worked because we didn't lead with the film. We led with the audience's experience of watching a horror trailer in a theatre: the anticipation, the darkness, the collective held breath of a crowd that's about to be scared. We understood that moment viscerally. And we built an idea that hijacked it in a way that felt completely organic.
p
When people shared the content, they weren't sharing a movie promotion. They were sharing something that made them feel something. That's the difference.
p

You could see it in how the clip travelled. The headlines led with the woman, not the film, and every one of them still carried the film's name. Spotting the marketing didn't stop anyone sharing it: one post that carried the clip, [quoted by SheThePeople](https://www.shethepeople.tv/viral-video/woman-acts-possessed-the-popes-exorcist), said the marketing team had taken "the scare factor to a whole new level."
h2
2. Cultural fluency beats production value every single time.
p

We didn't have a massive budget. We didn't have a celebrity. We didn't have a production crew or a fancy shoot. What we had was a deep understanding of how Indian audiences engage with horror, with cinema, with meme culture, and with the specific pleasure of being scared in a crowded theatre with strangers.
p

That cultural fluency, knowing what would make this specific audience stop scrolling, lean in and send it to their friends, was worth more than any production budget. I grew up watching films the way Indian audiences watch films: loudly, communally, emotionally. I knew what would land because I was the audience.
p

This is why I'm always sceptical of global brands that create one piece of content and try to push it across every market. Virality is local before it's global. It spreads because it feels like it was made for you specifically, not for everyone vaguely.
h2
3. The idea has to be willing to be uncomfortable.
p

Safe content does not go viral. I have never seen a perfectly polished, brand-approved, legal-reviewed, twelve-rounds-of-feedback piece of content genuinely break through. Not once. The content that travels is always the content that made someone in the approval chain a little bit nervous.
p

The Pope's Exorcist campaign had an edge to it. It was bold. It made people do a double-take. It wasn't the kind of content a large agency with a lot to lose would have approved in the first round. But WLDD was fifteen people with everything to gain and very little to protect, and that freedom was the creative advantage.
quote
If every idea gets smoothed down until it's inoffensive and forgettable, you are not making content. You're making wallpaper. And nobody shares wallpaper.
h2
4. Memes are not a tactic. They are a language.
p

At WLDD, meme marketing was at the core of how we thought about everything. Not because memes are "trendy", but because memes are how large portions of the internet actually communicate. They are cultural shorthand. They travel fast because they carry meaning efficiently, and they're participatory by nature: people remix them, respond to them, and pass them on.
p

The brands that treat memes as a tactic ("let's do a meme this week") almost always get it wrong. It feels forced because it is. The brands that understand meme culture as a living, breathing language, and speak it fluently and in real time, are the ones whose content actually gets shared by real people to other real people.
p

The Pope's Exorcist campaign spoke that language. It didn't just use a meme format. It understood the emotional grammar of how Indian internet culture reacts to horror, to cinema, to the unexpected. That's the difference between speaking a language and just knowing a few words.
h2
5. Speed matters more than perfection.
p

The internet moves fast. Cultural moments have a half-life measured in hours, sometimes minutes. One of the biggest advantages of being at a small, scrappy startup like early WLDD was that we could go from idea to execution in a fraction of the time a larger organisation would need. We could see a moment happening, make something about it, and be live before anyone else had finished their first internal approval email.
p

This is a structural problem for large brands, not a creative one. The people with the best ideas are usually close to the culture. They're young, they're online, they feel the moment in real time. But those people are often several layers away from anyone who can say yes fast enough for the moment to still be alive. By the time the idea gets approved, the moment has passed.
p

If you're building a brand or running a marketing team, the most valuable thing you can do is create a short approval path for real-time content. Trust the people who are closest to the culture. Give them room to move quickly. A good idea published in time beats a perfect idea published too late, every single time.
p

Virality is not a formula. It's not a checklist. It's not a budget line item. It's what happens when the right idea meets the right audience at the right moment, and someone was brave enough to make it without waiting for permission.
h2
Not a formula, but five questions worth asking
ul
**Who is it for, exactly?** Not "India" or "Gen Z". A room, a habit, a moment.
**What will they feel in the first three seconds?** If the answer is "informed", start again.
**Would they send it to a friend if your logo weren't in it?** If the only reason to share is the brand, it won't travel.
**Did it make anyone in the approval chain nervous?** A little nerves is a good sign.
**Can it go live while the moment is still alive?** If not, find a smaller idea that can.
h2
Mistakes I see brands make
ul
Putting the logo, tagline and product shot in the first frame of everything.
Making one piece of content and pushing it across every market.
Doing "a meme this week" instead of learning how their audience actually talks.
Running real-time ideas through a twelve-step approval process.
Mistaking reach for virality. Reach is bought. Virality is passed on.
h2
What happened after.
p

The campaign changed WLDD's trajectory. It changed mine too. It confirmed something I had always believed: that the principles of great filmmaking and the principles of great marketing are the same. Know your audience. Build to an emotion. Be specific. Be brave. Move fast.
p

Sony stayed. The work grew to cover [65](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65_%28film%29), [Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man:_Across_the_Spider-Verse) and [Insidious: The Red Door](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insidious:_The_Red_Door). The full campaign, with every piece of coverage, is in the [Pope's Exorcist case study](/work/the-popes-exorcist/).
p

I eventually left WLDD, at the peak of my time there, which I'd recommend to anyone, to pursue filmmaking full time in New York. I made the Dean's List at the New York Film Academy, shot [Love Is Stronger Than Hate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VQRsfpHgC38) as director of photography (it won Best Costume Design at the Follow Your Heart Film Festival), and founded [Thava Studio](https://www.instagram.com/thava.studio), a creative studio working with brands across New York, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and Bangalore.
p

Everything I build now, whether it's a social media strategy for a restaurant in Brooklyn, a short film shot on New York rooftops, or a content system for a luxury brand, runs on the same instincts I developed in that first WLDD office. The audience is always the film. The brand is always the character. The moment is always the script.
p

If you're building something right now and trying to figure out how to make it travel, stop asking how to go viral. Start asking what your audience actually feels, what cultural moment you're speaking into, and whether you're brave enough to say something worth sharing. The rest tends to follow.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**What was the Pope's Exorcist campaign in India?** A guerrilla cinema stunt by WLDD for Sony Pictures India in April 2023: a woman, apparently possessed, crawled through a real audience while the trailer played, and the filmed reaction went viral.
**What is guerrilla marketing?** Low-cost, unconventional marketing that surprises people in a real place, so their reaction becomes the message.
**What is meme marketing?** Brand communication written in the internet's own formats and humour and spread through meme pages and creators, so it travels like content rather than an ad.
**Can you make something go viral?** You can't guarantee it. You can raise the odds: build for one audience's real habits, lead with a feeling, accept some risk and publish while the moment is live.

title: Why I broke the 180-degree rule.
dek: One cell, one light, and a camera that switches sides when the power does. How and when to break the rule on purpose.

cover.alt: Agent X, an interrogation scene directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: Dillon Cain as the agent leans across a table toward Nathan Flores as the seated prisoner, under a single overhead light
cover.cap: Agent X. With Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores. Director of photography Yoey Garfield.

body: p
At the [New York Film Academy](https://www.nyfa.edu/), the production workshop is where you get a real studio, a crew and a dolly, and one scene to prove you can run a set. I built a prison cell.
p

The scene is Agent X. An agent visits a prisoner serving a life sentence and makes him an offer. The film around it was never shot, so here's the subtext: the offer is a second chance, if the prisoner signs his life over and works for the agent as a hitman. He'd be paid. He might die in the field. Either way, he'd be out.
yt
GSIja5IH9eo
Agent X
Agent X, an interrogation scene directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, with Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores
Watch the scene, 3 min
h2
The short version
ul
**The rule:** keep the camera on one side of the line between two characters, so the audience always knows who's where.
**The break:** in Agent X the camera crosses that line once, at the moment the prisoner says yes.
**The reason:** when the power in the room flips, the picture should flip with it.
**The kit:** a RED Komodo, one overhead light, dolly track on both sides of the table, a small crew and no budget.
h2
One cell, one light
p

We built the set inside the studio to look like a cell: one room, one table, lit from a single light above, with another light picking out the actors' heads. Faces fall in and out of shadow every time someone leans in. We laid dolly track on both sides of the table, so the camera could move with whoever held the power.
p

Yoey Garfield shot it on a [RED Komodo](https://www.red.com/komodo-6k), a compact 6K cinema camera. Dillon Cain played the agent and Nathan Flores the prisoner. Yoey and I swap seats: on his film [Love Is Stronger Than Hate](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt38273553/), I was his director of photography.
h2
The power is in the blocking
p

At the start, the agent stands and leans over the table while the prisoner sits. He's the one asking, so he's the one dominating. The prisoner keeps saying no. He's already rotting in there for life, so what could the agent possibly do for him?
p

The agent slides a granola bar across the table. By the midpoint the prisoner takes it and eats it. That's the first crack: he's starting to see that this offer is the only second chance he'll ever get.
h2
Why I crossed the line
p

Film school teaches the [180-degree rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/180-degree_rule) early. Draw an imaginary line between two characters and keep the camera on one side of it, so the audience never loses track of who's where. Cross it, and the cut feels wrong.
p

That's exactly why I crossed it. For most of the scene the camera stays on one side of the line, while the agent is in control. The moment the prisoner is convinced, the power flips, and so does the camera. You should feel something change before anyone says it out loud.
p
Nobody in my class understood the choice, and my professors didn't agree with it either. I shot it anyway. The rule exists to keep the audience settled, and at that moment I wanted them unsettled.
quote
The camera crosses the line at the exact moment he does.
h2
Kubrick crossed it first
p

I'm not the first director to do this on purpose. In [The Shining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shining_%28film%29), when Jack Torrance meets the ghost of Delbert Grady in the hotel bathroom, Stanley Kubrick cuts to the other side of the line and the two men seem to swap places. [No Film School's breakdown](https://nofilmschool.com/2017/05/when-to-break-180-degree-rule) reads it as a jarring cut that deepens the unease of the scene, and cinematographer David Mullen ASC [describes it](https://blog.frame.io/2016/08/01/180-degree-rule-and-when-to-break-it/) as wide shots "from both directions, a 180-degree flip, crossing the line."
p

Kubrick broke the rule because Jack's grip on reality was breaking. I broke it because the power in the room was changing hands. Different reasons, same tool: the cut feels wrong, and the audience feels it before they can explain it.
h2
How to break the 180-degree rule on purpose
ul
**Establish the line first.** The audience has to learn the geography before they can feel it change. In Agent X the camera holds one side for most of the scene.
**Cross on a story beat, not a whim.** Find the one moment the scene turns. Ours is the prisoner's yes.
**Cross once.** One break reads as a choice. Three read as a mistake.
**Build the set for it.** We laid dolly track on both sides of the table, so the camera had somewhere to go when the power flipped.

**Know your two ways across.** Move the camera over the line on screen, with a dolly or a character walking, and the audience travels with you. Cut straight across, and they feel the jolt. Pick the one the moment needs.
**Defend it in one sentence.** Mine: the camera crosses the line at the exact moment he does. If you can't say yours, keep the rule.
h2
What people noticed
p

The scene went up on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIja5IH9eo) in September 2025. One of the comments under it is about the performance, not the camera: "Nathan's acting as the prisoner makes the tension feel so real." That's the effect I was after. You feel the shift in the room without noticing the cut that caused it.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**What is the 180-degree rule?** A filmmaking guideline: draw an imaginary line between two characters and keep every camera on one side of it, so their left-right positions stay the same from shot to shot.
**Is breaking it a mistake?** Only when it's an accident. Broken on purpose, it unsettles the audience, which is why directors save it for hallucinations, betrayals and shifts in power.

**What is Agent X?** A three-minute interrogation scene I conceived and directed at a New York Film Academy production workshop, shot on a RED Komodo by Yoey Garfield, with Dillon Cain and Nathan Flores.
**Where can I watch it?** On [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSIja5IH9eo), or with my other shorts in the [films section](/#films).
p

Crew: director of photography Yoey Garfield, assistant director Yi Chan (Ethan), gaffer Yamira, grip Nicolas, sound Cito, first AC Jeff, second AC Ramon. Nathan and Ethan are also in [The Last Pizza](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3YfriOGVA4w), and how we work as a crew is in [How I make films in New York on an indie budget](/work/how-i-make-films-in-new-york-on-an-indie-budget/).

title: Hub, hype and hygiene.
dek: The posting mix behind every brand I've run.

cover.alt: Hub, hype and hygiene, the content mix used by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil: hub about half to 60% of posts, hype around 30%, hygiene 10 to 20%
cover.cap: The mix I start every account with. It moves with the brand.

body: p
Every brand I've run gets the same posting plan, from film and FMCG campaigns at WLDD in Bangalore to cafes in New York. I call it hub, hype and hygiene.
p
It solves the problem every small brand has: posting every day without running out of ideas, and without boring the people who already follow you.
p

I didn't invent the shape. Google's YouTube playbook for brands split content into hero, hub and hygiene, later renamed [hero, hub and help](https://thinkwithgoogle.com/marketing-strategies/video/build-a-content-plan). What I changed is the third H. Hero content is the big tentpole moment, and most brands I work with can't afford one every month. Trends, though, show up every week for free. So my third H is hype.
h2
The short version
ul
**Hub,** about half to 60% of posts: what you do, in your own world. It keeps the people who already follow you.
**Hype,** around 30%: the week's trend, rebuilt in your setting. It finds new people.
**Hygiene,** 10 to 20%: why you exist. It earns trust.
**Judge each H by its own number:** sends for hype, likes and watch time for hub, saves and DMs for hygiene.
h2
Hub: what you do, in your own world
p

Hub is the everyday posting: what the brand makes, what happens inside it, and the people who run it. For a cafe that's the menu, the space and the regulars. For a gym it's the workouts. It also covers anything shot in the brand's own surroundings, so a skit where the waiter plays a character is still hub, because it lives where the brand lives.
h2
Hygiene: why you exist
p

Hygiene keeps the mission visible. If a restaurant's promise is authentic Indian food, or authentic halal food, hygiene posts explain it: where the flavours come from, how a dish is made, what makes it the real thing. They're often simple, information-first posts or a talking head, and they're the posts people check before they decide to trust you.
h2
Hype: the trend, moved into your world
p
Hype is whatever is trending that week, a sound, a pop culture moment, a dance, rebuilt inside the brand's own setting. It's the fastest way to reach people who don't follow you yet.
h2
The mix
ul
Hub: about half to 60% of posts
Hype: around 30%
Hygiene: 10 to 20%, depending on the brand
p

The mix matters more than any single post. Post only hype and you run out of trends, and the audience forgets what you sell. I've seen a pet food brand whose page is all office trends, so people think it's an office company. Post only hub and nobody new finds you. Post only hygiene and it reads like a brochure. With a mix, you can post every day without the page getting saturated.
h2
How to build a week
p
This is how I set it up for a new account.
ul
Map the brand's world: the place, the products, the people. Every hub post comes from this list.
Write the mission in one sentence. Every hygiene post explains a piece of it.
Each week, collect the trends you could rebuild inside that world, and drop the ones you can't.
Fill the week by the mix, then shoot hub in batches, since it doesn't go stale.
Once a month, look at the numbers. If reach is flat, add hype. If new followers don't know what you sell, add hub.
h2
A week, as a template
p
Seven posts for a cafe, at roughly the mix above:
ul
Monday, hub: the drink of the week, made start to finish.
Tuesday, hype: this week's trending sound, acted out behind the counter.
Wednesday, hub: the people who run the place.
Thursday, hygiene: where the beans come from, and why it matters.
Friday, hub: a regular's order.
Saturday, hype: a pop culture moment, set in the cafe.
Sunday, hub: the space on a busy morning.
p
That's four hub, two hype and one hygiene. Swap in what your brand has, and keep the ratio.
p
Short on time? At three posts a week, make it two hub and one hype, and work a hygiene post in every other week.
h2
Where I've used it
p

Everywhere: film and OTT launches, FMCG, food and retail pages at WLDD, influencer pages and PR for actors, and through Thava Studio in America, cafes, restaurants and real estate. Four of the case studies show it working:
ul
[Fetchy](/work/fetchy/): the plan took YouTube Shorts from 600 to 1,000 views each to above 2,000, and one Short passed 616,000.
[Infamous Coconuts](/work/infamous-coconuts/): we rebuilt the feed around hub, hype and hygiene, and the typical reel went from about 5,000 views to 98,000.
[Thank You Durex](/work/thank-you-durex/): memes as hooks, with skits and trends built around the product. One reel passed 20.9 million views.
[WLDD's own Instagram](/work/wldd-instagram/): run as a client page with the office as the cast. In 2022, 8 of 82 reels passed 10,000 views. In my sixteen months, 56 of 100 did.
h2
What the research says
p

Two studies back up why hype stays at about 30% and not 100%. A 2023 study in the Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing found that brand memes build the relationship when they're easy to get, feel new and fit the brand, and that sarcasm works against them ([read the study](https://emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/JRIM-01-2023-0029/full/html)). Another, in the Journal of Consumer Marketing, found that meme posts read as funnier and earn more likes and shares, but lower engagement on cause-related campaigns ([read the study](https://www.emerald.com/jcm/article/doi/10.1108/JCM-09-2024-7221/1253616/Brand-posts-with-memes-on-social-media-perceived)). Humour travels, but it has to fit the brand and the moment.
p

Audiences say the same thing. The 2025 [Sprout Social Index](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/index/), a survey of more than 4,000 consumers in the US, UK, Canada and Australia, found that people want brands to understand the context of cultural moments, not recreate every meme, and [a third think it's embarrassing](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/press/the-days-of-trend-chasing-are-over-new-research-from-sprout-social-reveals-a-third-of-consumers-think-jumping-on-viral-trends-is-embarrassing-for-brands/) when brands jump on viral trends. That's the case for hype at around 30%, rebuilt inside your own world, instead of chasing every trend.
h2
How to measure each H
p

Each H has a different job, so judge each one by a different number. Instagram's Adam Mosseri has said the [signals that matter most in ranking](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/instagram-shares-algorithm-2025/738034/) are watch time, likes and sends, with likes counting a little more for people who already follow you and sends a little more for people who don't.
ul
Hype is for reach, so watch sends per reach. If nobody sends a trend post, it isn't reaching new people.
Hub is for the people who already follow you, so watch likes per reach and watch time.
Hygiene is for trust, so watch saves, profile visits and the questions people ask in DMs.
h2
Mistakes to avoid
ul
A trend with no bridge to your world. If you can't set it in your space, with your people or your product, skip it.
Hygiene that sounds like an ad. Explain, don't sell.
Judging the plan one post at a time. Look at the month.
Copying another brand's mix. A new account may need more hype to be found; a known brand may need more hub.
quote
If you post one kind of thing every day, the page gets saturated. Mix the three and you can keep posting.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**What is hub, hype and hygiene?** A posting mix for social media: hub is your everyday content, hype is trends rebuilt in your world, and hygiene explains why you exist. It adapts Google's hero, hub and hygiene model for YouTube.

**How often should a small brand post?** As often as you can keep up. At seven posts a week, try four hub, two hype and one hygiene. At three, make it two hub and one hype, with a hygiene post every other week.
**Should brands jump on every trend?** No. Take only the trends you can rebuild inside your own world, and keep hype to about a third of your posts.

title: How we plan a micro drama in a day.
dek: The AI production stack behind 12+ series.
short: Micro dramas, planned in a day

cover.alt: Close-up of an actress on a phone call in warm light, from Demo Day, a Canvas series directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, produced by Abhinav Singla, shot by Kais Vasaya
cover.cap: Still from [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/), a 10-episode Canvas series shot at Harvard in under four days.

body: p
We've planned shoots the night before and rolled camera the next morning. Cast confirmed, locations locked, call sheet out. Nobody panicked.
p

That isn't a flex about speed. It's the only way a micro drama works on a startup budget. This year I directed [12+ short-form series](/#series) for [Canvas](https://creatorsarethenewstudios.com/), a New York and Mumbai micro drama studio, shot across New York, Boston, Baltimore, San Francisco and Los Angeles. Most were shot in three or four days.
h2
The short version
ul
**Plan in Directure AI.** Script in; breakdown, shot cards, shoot days, call sheets and budget out, all linked to the same script.
**Finish in a Claude Code pipeline** connected to Premiere Pro, Higgsfield and ElevenLabs, trained on our own rules.
**Every shoot doubles as ad creative:** snippet ads, vox pops and fast recuts from performance data.
**AI buys back time.** People still choose the story, the face and the take.
p
Here's how each piece works, and what I've learned running it.
h2
Why micro dramas need a different production model
p
A micro drama episode runs under two minutes. A season is five to ten episodes. The budget is a fraction of a short film's, and the shoot is three or four days.
p
You can't spend a week in pre-production on a series that shoots in three days. The planning has to move as fast as the shoot.
p

There's a second constraint. Every Canvas series is creator-led: a creator with a real audience is attached from day one, like Ruhani Sharma (1.4M followers) on [Dear NYC](/series/dear-nyc/) or Robert Maxwell (1.1M) on [Red Flags](/series/red-flags/). Their calendar is the production calendar. When it moves, everything moves.
p

The format is worth the squeeze. Sensor Tower counted [$2.98 billion in in-app revenue](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/microdrama-apps-stand-out-on-mobile-heres-what-the-numbers-say/812610/) for micro and short drama apps in 2025, up 115% on the year before, and in the first quarter of 2025 [the US alone brought in 49%](https://sensortower.com/blog/state-of-short-drama-apps-2025) of it. The audience is on the phone, and it's growing faster than any production schedule.
h2
Step 1: Plan everything in Directure AI
p
We plan most of our series in [Directure AI](https://directureai.com/), a production planning platform built in New York by Abhinav Singla and his team.
p

You upload the script and it breaks it down: characters, locations, props, wardrobe and scene requirements. AI Boarding turns scenes into shot cards and suggests how each shot should be made. From there you build shoot days, call sheets and a budget, all connected to the same script.
p

The real win isn't the breakdown. It's what happens when the script changes. You see right away what a rewrite does to the schedule and the budget, so we rewrite for logistics, not just story. If two scenes can share a location, they do. If a scene needs a fourth shoot day, it gets cut or moved.
p

When the plan breaks anyway, the script should already know what to do. On Demo Day, every scene heading listed a primary location and pre-approved backups, so losing a location never meant a rewrite.
p
Two examples:
ul

[Demo Day](/series/demo-day/): 10 episodes at Harvard and around Boston in under four days. On the morning we left New York, our lead actor had to drop out. We recast that morning, rewrote the role in the car on the drive up, and wrote each day's episodes around what we'd already shot. [Here's the full story of that shoot](/work/ten-episodes-at-harvard-in-under-four-days/).

[Face Value](/series/face-value/): a four-part micro documentary shot inside New York Fashion Week. The world was already there, so we built no sets and spent nothing on production design. [Watch Face Value on Canvas](https://www.canvasott.com/video/cmw1t94ey00kxs60ek9qkz9gt).
h2
Step 2: A Claude Code pipeline for post-production
p
Post is where most short-form budgets quietly die. Ten episodes means ten edits, ten sets of graphics, ten rounds of notes.
p

I run [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) with agents connected to [Premiere Pro](https://www.adobe.com/products/premiere.html), [Higgsfield](https://higgsfield.ai/) and [ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io/). It handles the repetitive layers: assembling selects, building animations and infographics, generating AI shots where a live shot isn't possible, and temp voice. One series, Made in the Valley, was produced end to end this way.
p

The tool isn't the advantage. Everyone can buy the same subscription. The advantage is the training. I've spent months teaching my setup our scripts, our edit rules, our hooks and our revision notes as reusable skills. Each production makes it better at the next one.
p

One rule we don't break: it can't look like AI. You can usually tell when something was made with a default setup, so we feed it as many references as we can, and every output goes through a human edit.
h2
Step 3: Every shoot becomes ad creative
p
A series isn't finished when it's uploaded. It's finished when people watch it.
p
So every shoot also produces marketing:
ul
Snippet ads cut from the strongest few seconds of each episode
Organic vox pops and talking heads filmed on the same days
Fast revisions from performance data: which hook held, which didn't, and new cuts built around the winners
p
Each show is also packaged for its creator's audience, so it travels on Instagram and YouTube as well as the app.
h2
What AI doesn't do
p
It doesn't choose the story. It doesn't cast the face that makes you stop scrolling. It doesn't know when a take is true.
p

What it does is buy back time for those decisions. On a three-day shoot, the hours we save in planning and post are the hours we spend on performance, on the hook, and on the cliffhanger that sells the next episode.
p
Speed also exposes weak scripts faster. When you can plan a shoot in a day, there's nowhere for a bad idea to hide.
h2
A one-day planning checklist
ul
**Lock the creator's dates first.** Everything else is built around them.
**Upload the script, then check the breakdown by hand.** The tool is fast, not infallible.
**Rewrite for logistics.** Merge scenes that can share a location, and cut or move anything that needs an extra day.
**Give every scene a backup location.**
**Build shoot days, then the call sheet,** from the same plan, so a change in one updates the other.
**Schedule the marketing shots on the same days:** the snippet moments, vox pops and talking heads.
**Set up the edit before the shoot,** with your hooks, graphics rules and revision notes ready.
h2
Mistakes to avoid
ul
Spending a week in pre-production on a three-day shoot.
Treating the creator's calendar as flexible. It's the production calendar.
Letting AI output go out without a human edit.
Finishing the series and only then thinking about how people will find it.
h2
Quick answers
ul
**What is a micro drama?** A scripted series made for the phone, with episodes of a minute or two that each end on a hook. A season is usually five to ten episodes.

**What is Directure AI?** A production planning platform built in New York by Abhinav Singla and his team. It breaks a script into characters, locations, props and wardrobe, turns scenes into shot cards, and builds shoot days, call sheets and budgets from the same script.
**How do you use AI in production without it looking like AI?** Use it for the repetitive layers, feed it as many references as you can, and put every output through a human edit.
**How long does a micro drama take to shoot?** Most of the 12+ series I've directed for Canvas were shot in three or four days.
p

Your turn: what's the one part of production you'd hand to AI first, and the one part you'd never hand over? [Tell me in the comments on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/how-we-plan-micro-drama-day-ai-production-stack-12-thavarayil-zkpte/). I read every comment.

title: Ten episodes at Harvard in under four days.

body: p
In August we shot a 10-episode web series at Harvard in under four days, and it turned into one of the wildest shoots I've been part of.
p

It started with Abhinav Singla, owner of [Directure AI](https://directureai.com/), getting a pitch slot at Harvard. He asked if we could turn the whole trip into something more. We said yes before we had a script. The idea was two roommate founders building an AI-powered filmmaking tool, pitching it to investors, and the real Harvard pitch would become the final episode of the series.
p
We had a baseline idea and three days to shoot it.
h2
The short version
ul
**What:** [Demo Day](/series/demo-day/), a ten-episode startup web series shot guerrilla style around Harvard.
**How fast:** under four days of 17-hour shoots, each episode written around what we'd shot the day before.
**What went wrong:** our lead actor dropped out the morning we left, and we missed the real pitch.
**What saved it:** an actor who said yes in one phone call, a crew who did every job, and a script built to bend.
h2
The script we drove up with
p

By the time we left, the baseline idea had become a master script with the working title The Problem Statement: ten episodes, each with a one-line hook written above it. Episode two: "Four hours by hand. Thirty seconds by machine." Episode eight: "He's deleting a $29 subscription. It was never about the $29."
p

It was written to survive a shoot like this. Every scene heading listed a primary location and pre-approved backups, so a bench we couldn't use never meant a rewrite. Every text message on screen was tagged with how to shoot it, mostly as real screen recordings. The laptops ran the real Directure, so we needed no motion graphics. The only other voice in the story, a first customer called Marcus, was written to be performed live on a real phone call from off camera, so the reactions would be real.
p

It even had a running gesture between the two founders, a four-beat handshake called the checkmark: clasp, hold, draw a checkmark in the air, knuckle tap. It came back seven times, fumbled in episode two and finally finished after the pitch in episode ten.
p
What it couldn't plan for was losing half its cast. Every role lived inside the two founders, which made the series cheap to shoot and fragile to cast.
h2
The morning we were supposed to leave
p

Our lead actor stopped answering his phone. We called for hours with nothing back. We pushed our 9am pitch to the afternoon and started driving anyway, hoping he'd still show up. He did, for about twenty minutes, before telling us he had a family emergency and had to turn around and go home.
p
So now we had no actor, no backup, four hours from New York, and ten episodes still to shoot.
p

I called every actor I knew in the city. Nobody could clear four days on a few hours' notice. Abhinav ended up calling someone he'd only met once, at a workshop months earlier. Her name is Chewie. She picked up, heard the pitch, and said yes without hesitating for a second. We rewrote her entire role in the car on the drive up.
p
We missed the actual pitch. We ended up faking it in an empty auditorium the next day, just to get the footage we needed.
h2
Four days, written backwards
p
What followed was four days of 17-hour shoots, sleeping two hours at a time, and writing each episode based on what we'd already shot the day before, because there was never time to write it first.
p

Everyone did a bit of everything. Abhinav was acting and producing, Kais Vasaya was shooting as director of photography, and at different points all of us were writing, art directing, or just throwing out ideas because that's what the day needed.
h2
What a four-day series teaches you
ul
**Write the alternates into the script.** A primary location and a backup or two in every scene heading turns a decision on the day into seconds, not a meeting.
**Shoot what can't be repeated first.** Our first day was built around the real event, because it only happens once. When we missed it, staging it in an empty auditorium the next day was the fix.
**Keep the cast tiny, but know your second call.** Two leads made the shoot cheap. It also meant one unanswered phone nearly ended it.
**Give every episode a one-line hook.** If you can't write the hook, the episode isn't ready. On a phone, the hook is the episode.
**Put the real product on screen.** A screen recording of a real tool is faster than motion graphics and more convincing.
**Plant a motif early and pay it off late.** One repeated gesture, spaced across the season, gives a short series an ending that feels earned.
**When the plan breaks, write from the footage.** Each day's rushes became the next day's outline. That's how we finished the season.
quote
Ten episodes, no real plan, and honestly one of the best things I've made this year.
h2
The people who made it
p

Abhinav Singla produced and starred. Kais Vasaya was director of photography. Chewie stepped in on a few hours' notice and played a role rewritten for her in the car. I directed, and like everyone else I wrote, art directed and threw out ideas wherever the day needed them.
h2
Quick answers
ul

**What is Demo Day?** A ten-episode startup web series directed by Nivedkrishna Thavarayil, about two roommate founders building an AI filmmaking tool, shot around Harvard in under four days in August 2026.
**What is Directure AI?** Abhinav Singla's AI production planning tool. It plays itself in the series.
**How do you shoot a series in four days?** Plan alternates for every scene, keep the cast small, shoot the moments you can't repeat first and write each day from the last day's footage.
p

This is the shoot I think about when people ask how we plan a series so fast. [Here's the system we use now](/work/how-we-plan-a-micro-drama-in-a-day/), and [here's the series page for Demo Day](/series/demo-day/).

body: p
I didn't cold email a database. I didn't run ads. I didn't have a sales deck. I just talked to people.
p

My co-founder [Agrajh Ak](https://www.linkedin.com/in/agrajh-ak/) and I just signed our biggest client to date at [Growvior](https://www.instagram.com/growvior/): a $10,000 engagement with a New York-based tech startup that is building something genuinely exciting in the South Asian and Asian community here in America. They are founding-stage. They came to us because they needed a software partner who understood their vision from day one.
p

I'm not going to tell you the client details. That's their story to tell when they're ready. What I am going to tell you is exactly how we got here. Because it has nothing to do with cold outreach funnels, LinkedIn automation tools, or any growth hack you've read about in a newsletter.
p
It has everything to do with one thing: talking to people.
h2
The short version
ul
**No cold email, no ads, no deck.** Our biggest Growvior client came from a conversation.
**Tell people everything you do.** You never know which part someone has been looking for.
**Referrals are a chain,** and every link starts with one honest conversation.
**Your online presence pitches** when you're not in the room.
**Start before you're ready.** Mistakes are how you learn to price, promise and deliver.
h2
Stop waiting for someone to ask. Just tell them what you do.
p

I run two companies. [Thava Studio](https://www.instagram.com/thava.studio/), a creative agency handling social media strategy, content production and brand direction for clients across New York, Los Angeles, Philadelphia and Bangalore. And [Growvior](https://growvior.com/), the AI-integrated software company Agrajh and I started in Kochi in 2025, building products for clients in New York and India. I'm also a filmmaker. My work spans restaurants in Brooklyn, vocal coaches, realtors, EdTech platforms, fashion model PR, a film production house and now a founding-stage tech startup.
p
When I tell people this, the most common reaction is: "Wait, you do all of that?"
p
Yes. And I never hide any of it. Because you never know which part of what you do is the exact thing someone in the room has been looking for.
p

Maybe the real estate agent you meet at a dinner needs a website. Maybe the DJ you bump into at a film screening has no idea how to grow his Instagram. Maybe the cafe owner you chat with at a coffee shop has been trying to figure out how to make reels that actually get views. Maybe the app founder in your network has built something great but has no social media strategy to get it to market. Maybe the graphic designer you follow online needs someone to handle their email marketing and client proposals.
p

All of these people exist. I have found every single one of them, not through a CRM, not through paid ads, but through genuine conversation. Through asking questions, listening properly, and then saying: "Actually, that's something I can help with."
h2
What Growvior actually does
p

When I bring up Growvior, this is the picture I want in people's heads: a small, focused team of builders, designers and thinkers, working in four areas. Custom software, creative media and branding, website development, and mobile apps for iOS and Android.
p

In February 2026, Growvior was [accepted into the Google for Startups Cloud Program](https://www.instagram.com/growvior/p/DVLRPeVDsg1/), Google's [program for early-stage startups](https://cloud.google.com/startup), which gives us cloud credits, expert support and resources for the AI products we build.
